open-question.question: Some occurrences of the word milestone stay by decision after the rename (the CHANGELOG's entries, the `milestone_NN` directory names and the numbered milestones `CLAUDE.md` cites for its measurements), so a search that finds nothing cannot be the bar, and the test suites pin behaviour, not vocabulary: a leftover in runtime prose, in the docs, or in a help text no test quotes fails nothing. How is the rename known to be complete: by a listed residue a test checks, by a listed residue checked once by hand when the work ends, or by no bar beyond the drift gate and the suites?
open-question.alternative: A permanent check over the runtime surface only, `core/` and thereby every rendered host tree, written as a build check beside `host-name-in-core` in `scripts/build_hosts.py` (or as a pytest over the same files), with a residue list that is empty or nearly so. The rest of the tree (the docs, `CLAUDE.md`, the README and CONTRIBUTING, `tests/`, `host_tests/`, `.github/`, `.claude/`, `ideas/`) is checked once by hand when the work ends: a search run in the last task and compared against a residue list recorded in the milestone. A permanent guard covers the files runners actually follow and costs almost no exemptions, since `core/` keeps nearly nothing of the old word by decision, and an existing check shows the pattern for a vocabulary scan of `core/`. The mixed, residue-heavy files are checked once against a list without being held to that list forever. It means two mechanisms and two lists. A leftover reintroduced later into the docs, `CLAUDE.md`, or a test name fails nothing, and the one-time check's thoroughness depends on how carefully the last task runs it.

A permanent pytest under `tests/` that searches every tracked file (build output and `uv.lock` aside, or the rendered host trees included) for the word in any capitalisation and fails on any occurrence the listed residue in the test does not cover. The residue is listed at two grains: whole paths kept as written (such as `CHANGELOG.md`) and patterns kept wherever they stand (such as the `milestone_NN` directory names and the citations of numbered milestones in `CLAUDE.md`). It runs in both suite runs and in CI, and it stays after the work ends. A leftover anywhere, in runtime prose, a help text, the docs, or a template, fails the suite on the run that brings it in, now and on every later edit, the same way `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` holds the console lines to their table, so completeness is checked mechanically rather than asserted. It bans a common English word from the repository for good: every later legitimate use (a release note about the rename, a retired form a `CLAUDE.md` invariant names, a quoted older commit) needs an entry in the list, and whole-path entries cannot be used for mixed files such as `CLAUDE.md`, so the patterns have to be precise or a leftover passes inside an exempt line. What the list holds depends on what the sibling questions on the idea drafts, the principle store's path and text, the hard-cut invariant entry, and the upgrade guidance leave in place.

The same permanent check over `core/` (and so every rendered host tree), as a build check or pytest with an empty or near-empty residue list, and nothing beyond it, the drift gate, and the suites. No residue list is kept for the rest of the tree and no search is run there when the work ends. The surface whose leftovers mislead a runner is guarded for good at the lowest cost, with no hand step and no list to keep for the files that hold the residue by decision. A leftover in the docs, `CLAUDE.md`, the templates under `.github/`, the release skill, or the host suite fails nothing, either now or later, so a hard cut that is meant to leave `main` consistent under the new word has nothing showing that it does outside `core/`.

No new test or build check. The residue (the paths and patterns that keep the word by decision) is listed in the milestone, and the last task runs one whole-tree search for the word in any capitalisation and checks that every hit is on the list, so the completion's verified bar records the result. Completeness is checked across the whole tree against a stated list, with no permanent code, no ban on the word after the work ends, and no list to maintain in later milestones, and the verified bar of the last task's `Task-completion:` commit holds the evidence. The check happens once. A leftover added after the last task, or by the plugin rename's work that follows on the same files, fails nothing, and because the check runs only at the end, tasks done earlier get no mechanical feedback while the work goes on.

A whole-tree residue test with its listed residue, as in the whole-tree option, added in the work's first task so that each later task's suite runs execute it, then removed in the last task once it passes. After the work, nothing beyond the drift gate and the suites remains. Every task gets the same mechanical check while the rename is under way, so a task that misses a file or reintroduces the word is caught when it runs rather than at the end, and the repository is left with no lasting ban on the word. The test is written and then deleted within one piece of work, so its list is built in full for a check nobody keeps. After it is removed, a later leftover fails nothing, which leaves the same gap as the one-time hand check, at more cost.

No central residue list and no test. Each task that renames an area has, in its acceptance bar, a search for the word over the files that task covers, and the bar names any occurrences the task keeps by decision. Completeness is the sum of the task bars. It needs no extra artifact or end step. The completion procedure already derives a bar per task, and the check sits next to the edit that it verifies, so each area's exemptions are decided by the runner that knows the area. Coverage is only as complete as the task breakdown. A file no task names, such as a template, a slot value, or a test helper, is never searched, and with no whole-tree list the decisions on what remains are spread across commit bodies and nothing ever checks them together.

No residue list and no extra check: the rename is complete when the drift gate (`build_hosts.py --check`) and both pytest runs pass, together with the identifier-level tests that already pin vocabulary indirectly, the fixed console lines table and the fixed-call tests. A leftover found later is fixed as an ordinary stale sentence. It costs nothing and imposes no permanent vocabulary rule. The identifiers whose loss would break a run (the flag, the markers, the console lines, the tool interfaces, the skill names) are already pinned by tests that change together with them. A leftover in runtime prose, a help text no test quotes, the docs, or `CLAUDE.md` passes without notice. In a runner-facing file this is an instruction pointing at a form the hard cut no longer accepts, and nothing shows that the goal's "main consistent under the new word" holds.

open-question.question: The hard cut gives an existing project no migration: a live milestone under a `milestones/` container and the pointer-era state release 1.9.0 left (`milestones/README.md`, numbered directories) are read by nothing in the renamed plugin. Does the documentation this work rewrites say what such a project does at the upgrade, such as finishing its live milestones first or moving a directory by hand, or does it describe only the new shape and leave the upgrade to the release notes written by the plugin rename's work?
open-question.alternative: This work's documentation states the upgrade, in `docs/workflow.md`'s bootstrap paragraph, in the place of the sentence that now sends a pointer-era project to `/migrate-milestones`. The guidance is one rule: finish every live milestone with the copy of the plugin it was started under before upgrading. The pointer-era state (`milestones/README.md`, the numbered directories, the `## Milestone Workflow` section) is described as read by nothing, left in place, and removable by hand. No recipe for moving a directory by hand is given. The release notes are not relied on. It replaces the one sentence the removal of `/migrate-milestones` leaves wrong with the smallest true statement of the upgrade, and puts it beside the bootstrap, where an existing project's first step is described. It also matches the draft's position that the notes announce the rebranding and the documentation describes everything else the release changed. `docs/workflow.md` lives in the source repository, not in the distribution README a user installing the plugin reads, so the rule is easy to miss at the moment of upgrading. And because `VERSION` is 1.9.0 and the path-addressed form was never released, finishing "under the old copy" means a pointer-era finish for a released user and a finish from an unreleased `main` for anyone else, so the one rule has to name two different starting points.

This work's documentation states the upgrade in `docs/workflow.md`'s bootstrap paragraph, in the place of the `/migrate-milestones` sentence, and gives two paths. The first is to finish every live milestone under the old copy first. The second is to move a live milestone's directory by hand to `<scope>/mission_<slug>/`, with what that costs: the tool's log reads follow no rename, so the moved mission loses its `Starting-state:` anchor and reads as defined until its task list is next written. The pointer-era state is described as read by nothing and removable by hand. The release notes are not relied on. A project whose live milestone is part-way through is given a way to carry it across without finishing it early, and the losses the move brings are stated rather than found later. The guidance stands where the bootstrap and the old migration are already described. The hand move serves only projects running the unreleased path-addressed `main`, since no release ever shipped a `milestones/` container. Documenting it widens the hard cut's "no migration" into a supported manual migration whose correctness no test covers: an anchor to be re-established by re-running the starting state, and a scope the moved mission no longer holds. It is also the least visible place for a user upgrading from an install.

This work's documentation states the upgrade in a dedicated upgrade section of `README.md` and of each host's README template under `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, following the precedent of the templates' existing "Migrating from the old marketplace" section. `docs/workflow.md`'s `/migrate-milestones` sentence is replaced by a pointer to that section. The guidance is the finish-first rule alone, with the pointer-era state described as read by nothing and removable by hand, and no hand-move recipe. The release notes are not relied on. The guidance reaches the user where they install and update, on the landing page and in each published distribution tree, so a project holding old state learns before upgrading what it must do first. The README templates are exactly what the plugin rename's work rewrites next: for the new name, for the distribution repositories, and for what the old README says to a user arriving at the old name. A section written here is likely to be rewritten or merged there. It also adds a section to four files in place of changing one sentence.

This work's documentation states the upgrade in a dedicated upgrade section of `README.md` and of each host's README template, with `docs/workflow.md`'s `/migrate-milestones` sentence replaced by a pointer to it. It gives both paths: finish every live milestone under the old copy first, or move its directory by hand to `<scope>/mission_<slug>/`, with the lost `Starting-state:` anchor and the reset to defined stated. The pointer-era state is described as read by nothing and removable by hand. The release notes are not relied on. It is the most complete and most visible guidance: every user meets it at install time, and a user with a part-way milestone gets a way to keep it. It combines the costs of the two choices it is built from. It puts a hand-move recipe in public, published READMEs, a manual migration offered to a population (released 1.9.0 users) that can never hold a `milestones/` container, against a hard cut decided on the ground that Cairn was not widely adopted. And the section lands in the files the plugin rename's work rewrites next.

This work's documentation states, in `docs/workflow.md` where the `/migrate-milestones` sentence stands, only the fact of the hard cut as it bears on a project: a milestone under a `milestones/` container, `milestones/README.md`, and the numbered directories are read by nothing in the renamed plugin, and a milestone live there is invisible to it. It prescribes no path, neither finishing first nor moving by hand. The release notes are not relied on. It documents the limit the way the draft says the hard cut's limits are documented, in the same register as the record's documented start at the first `Task-completion:` commit, without committing the docs to an upgrade procedure nobody tests. It tells the reader what breaks but not what to do about it. A project with a live milestone has to work out the finish-first path itself, and may find it only after upgrading, when finishing under the old copy means reinstalling it.

This work's documentation describes only the new shape. The `/migrate-milestones` sentence in `docs/workflow.md` is removed with nothing in its place, and no file this work rewrites says what a project holding old state does at the upgrade. Whether and how that is said is left, later, to the plugin rename's work: its CHANGELOG entry and release notes, or what its README says to a user arriving at the old name. That work may also say nothing. This work's edits stay a pure rename of what exists, with no new section and no guidance written twice. The upgrade is told once, if at all, by the work that writes the one release every user upgrades through and that already settles what the old README says. The draft records that the release's notes announce the rebranding only and that the documentation describes everything else the release changed. Leaving the upgrade to the notes therefore leaves it to a place the draft has already scoped away from it. Until that work runs, `main` documents no upgrade path for a project with a live milestone, and whether anything is said at all depends on the plugin rename's work.

open-question.question: `CLAUDE.md` records the design decisions a later editor must not undo, often by naming a retired form with a ban on restoring it. Does it gain such an entry for the hard cut, naming the retired forms (the `milestones/` container, the `--milestone` flag, the `Milestone-definition:` and `Milestone-finish:` markers, `/migrate-milestones`) as never to be accepted or read again, which keeps the old word in the file by decision, or does it describe only the new shape?
open-question.alternative: `CLAUDE.md` gains one dedicated entry for the hard cut, written only in the new vocabulary and naming no retired form. It states the rule positively: the plugin answers to its current names only, through one flag, one discovery pattern (`**/mission_*/requirements.md`), and one finish marker. There is no alias and no second pattern, the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, and no migration is shipped. It gives the low-adoption ground as the reason. The decision and its reason are recorded where later editors look for what must not be undone, and the file adds no occurrence of the old word, so the hard cut adds nothing to the residue the sibling completeness bar has to account for. A ban that names nothing cannot be found by searching for the thing it bans. An editor working from a bug report that quotes `--milestone` or `Milestone-finish:` has to recognise for themselves that "one flag, no alias" covers it, which is weaker protection than the file gives every other retired form.

`CLAUDE.md` gains one dedicated invariant entry for the hard cut. It names each retired form literally (the `milestones/` container and its `**/milestones/*/requirements.md` pattern, the `--milestone` flag, the `Milestone-definition:` and `Milestone-finish:` markers, `/migrate-milestones`) and bans accepting, reading, or restoring any of them, with no alias, no second discovery pattern, and no migration. It records that the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, gives the one ground the draft records (Cairn was not widely adopted), and takes the place of the `migrate-milestones` invariant, which goes with its skill. The old word stays in that entry by decision. It follows the file's own pattern for retired forms: the seven "must not be restored" bans and the pre-split entry name what they retire. An editor who greps for `--milestone` or `Milestone-finish:` because a user reports an old project finds the ban and its reason in one place, so a well-meant alias or compatibility reader is stopped before it is written. It keeps the old word in `CLAUDE.md` permanently, as residue that has to be listed and told apart from a leftover however the sibling rename-completeness bar is set. The named forms can also read as live vocabulary to a runner that skims the file.

`CLAUDE.md` gains one dedicated entry that names the retired forms literally, as the first option does. It records the cut as a stated limit of the current design rather than a permanent ban: the renamed plugin accepts and reads none of the old forms and promises no reader or migration, the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, and a later milestone may add an upgrade path if adoption shows the need, in the way the existing `Tasklist-completion:` note leaves its commits unread "with no later reader promised". The old word stays in that entry by decision. It keeps the reason and the named forms findable in one place without closing a door the low-adoption ground may not justify closing for good. A later migration, if one is ever wanted, is then a revision of a recorded limit, not the reversal of a ban. A limit invites the very compatibility work the goal rules out: an editor reading "may add" can treat an alias or a dual reader as an open gap and fill it piecemeal. It also keeps the old word in the file as listed residue, the same cost as the first option.

No dedicated entry. Each existing invariant that owns a site the cut touches gains one clause naming the retired form it dropped and banning its return: the resolution invariant names the dropped `--milestone` flag, the read-only tool's invariant names the old discovery pattern and the `Milestone-finish:` marker and records that the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, the definition invariant names the `milestones/` container and `Milestone-definition:`, and the commit invariant notes that `/migrate-milestones` and its `--date` caller are gone. The old word stays in each of those clauses by decision. Each ban sits where an editor changing that site already reads, as the read-only tool's invariant already notes its own record limit beside the query it limits, so it protects the edit most likely to bring a form back. The old word is scattered across several entries instead of standing in one, which makes the residue harder to list and check. The single reason for the cut is either repeated at each site or stated nowhere whole.

No dedicated entry, and no retired form named. Each invariant that owns an affected site states its own rule in the new vocabulary with an exclusive "only": the resolution invariant says only `--mission` is recognised, the read-only tool's invariant says it reads `Mission-finish:` subjects and the one `mission_*` pattern only and that the record starts at the first `Mission-finish:` commit, and the definition invariant says the mission stands directly in its scope with no container. The cut is never described as a cut. The limits are stated where they apply and are checkable against each tool's contract, and `CLAUDE.md` gains no occurrence of the old word anywhere. Nothing records that a compatibility path was weighed and refused, or why. An "only" reads as a description of today rather than a decision, so a later alias or migration looks like an extension, not an undoing, and grepping for an old name finds nothing.

`CLAUDE.md` records nothing of the hard cut: no entry, no clause, and no exclusive wording beyond describing the new shape as it is. The `migrate-milestones` invariant and every other mention of the old forms are removed, and the decision is recorded only in this milestone's `## Decisions`, in `ideas/gurita.md`, and in whatever the documentation and help text say about where the record starts. This is permanent, not a postponement. The file stays a description of the plugin as it is, with no old word and nothing extra for the completeness bar to list. A hard cut on a little-adopted plugin arguably needs no guard, since there are few users whose reports would prompt a compatibility path. The file whose job is to stop a later editor undoing a design decision would be silent on one of the largest decisions this release makes. The places it would live instead are weak: `ideas/` drafts may be revised or dropped, and this milestone's decisions survive only at its finish commit's parent, which `summary` and `show` reach only if the sibling own-finish question makes that commit a `Mission-finish:` one.

open-question.question: The on-demand host suite is owed a passing run against each host whose trigger set a change touches, and this rename touches all three hosts' sets: slot value files and README templates in each host's definition, `core/agents/*.md`, and `host_tests/` itself. The plugin rename that follows directly touches the same sets again. Is the host suite run and passed on all three hosts within this work, or is that run left to the plugin rename's work?
open-question.recommendation: The suite compares the installed copy with the built tree, so a Claude Code run against the renamed tree before the finish would mean switching the served copy early; nothing is released between the two renames, and the plugin rename touches every trigger set again, so it owes the passing runs on all three hosts by the standing rule and its release gate requires them, while a run here would verify a state no user installs.
open-question.alternative: Timing: no host suite run in this work at all; the plugin rename's work, which touches the same trigger sets directly after, owes and makes the one round of passing runs covering both renames. Hosts: none here, all three there. Pays the three-host install-and-run round once for two back-to-back renames that ship in one release with nothing released between them, so no run is spent verifying a state no user will ever install. Breaks the stated rule outright: `main` stands with `host_tests/`, the agent files, and every host definition changed and unverified on any host until the next work runs, a failure found then cannot be told apart between the two renames, and if the plugin rename slips or is reshaped the debt has no owner.

Timing: before each commit of this work that touches a trigger set, as `CONTRIBUTING.md` ## Development states the rule. Hosts: every host whose set that commit touches, which is all three for any commit touching `core/agents/*.md`, `scripts/build_hosts.py`, or `host_tests/`, and the one host for a commit touching only that host's definition directory. Each run passes before its commit lands; nothing is left to the plugin rename's work. Follows the stated rule exactly, so the work sets no precedent of skipping it, and a failure is pinned to the one commit that caused it rather than traced back across the whole rename. The costliest position: a hard-cut rename lands as many commits, each touching shared paths, and every Antigravity and Codex run first needs the built tree copied or installed by hand into that host's installed location, since the suite stops when the copy differs from the committed tree; it also forces the tasks to be ordered so that every intermediate commit leaves the tools, the skills, and `host_tests/` (which itself invokes `--milestone`, writes `Milestone directory:` lines, and builds `Milestone-definition:` and `Milestone-finish:` commits) consistent enough to pass, which a half-renamed tree may not be; and the plugin rename pays the same three-host runs again directly after.

Timing: before each commit of this work that touches a trigger set. Hosts: Claude Code only, whose installed copy is the working tree's `hosts/claude/` under the directory marketplace and so is current after each rebuild with no install step. Antigravity and Codex: not run in this work; their runs are left to the plugin rename's work. Timing: once, after the last renaming change and before the milestone is finished, against the tree `main` ends in, rather than before each commit. Hosts: all three, each brought up to date by its documented install and run until it passes. Nothing is left to the plugin rename's work. Verifies on every host exactly the state this work promises to leave, `main` consistent under the new word, while sparing the intermediate half-renamed commits a bar they cannot meet and paying each host's install and run once. Bends the per-commit letter of the rule for the commits in between, so a failure found at the end has to be traced across the whole rename; the three-host cost is still paid twice in a row, once here and once by the plugin rename touching the same sets; and whether the Claude Code copy compared is the working tree at the run depends on which copy runs this milestone, an axis the running-copy question owns.

Timing: once, after the last renaming change and before the milestone is finished. Hosts: Claude Code only.
